name: Greenish Brown
lede: Greenish brown is a descriptive name for a dark olive-brown, and it appears in the naturalists' color lists that Baty reproduces; what the books say about it is modest and mostly about dyes and earths.

sections.title: A descriptive name
sections.body:
Greenish brown is not a pigment or a place; it describes a brown leaning toward green [1]. It is the last entry in a run of brown terms, after [[nut-brown]], liver brown and blackish brown, in a list reproduced in the introduction to Baty's study of naturalists' color lists [1]. Its nearest named relatives today are [[olive-brown]], [[olive]] and [[umber]] [6].

For materials the books use it as a plain description. Umber deposits range from dark brown to greenish brown [2], and tanning-extract experiments produced a range of browns, with iron salts giving greenish brown and tin brownish yellow [3].

sections.title: Khaki and the dye shortage
sections.body: The best-documented use is military. Cotton cloth in India was called khaki, the earth color, and through the 1800s it was chiefly a military cloth for soldiers' uniforms [4]. Army khaki of the First World War was typically bleached cotton re-dyed with chemical colors to a greenish brown [4]. In 1914 the German army was cut off from those dyes, and the shortage pushed German dye-making forward [4]. See [[khaki]] for the color itself.

sections.title: Jealousy and the aura
sections.body: One old text on psychic emanations says a greenish brown aura means jealousy [5]. Birren reports the claim as part of a catalogue of color meanings, not as evidence; colors do not carry one fixed emotion [5]. The same book lists greenish brown among skin tints seen in the late stages of some illnesses, which describes a complexion, not a diagnosis [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive this color is present in 308 paintings, 1.3 percent of 23,781, more common than 67 percent of named colors, as photographed [6]. It peaks in the 1800s, in 86 of 8,345 paintings (1.0 percent), about 1.4 times the expected rate [6]. The earliest match is a 1308 panel by Duccio, though the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first [6]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent [6]. It is most over-represented in Indian paintings, 2.6 times expected (13 of 721) [6].
